title: Sikorsky S-61N · Weaverville, CA (2008)
summary: The Safety Board's full report is available at http://www.ntsb.gov/publictn/A_Acc1.htm. The Aircraft Accident Report number is NTSB/AAR-10-06. On August 5, 2008, about 1941 Pacific daylight time, a Sikorsky S-61N helicopter, N612AZ, impacted trees and terrain during the initial climb after takeoff from Helispot 44 (H-44), located at an elevation of about 6,000 feet in mountainous terrain near Weaverville, California.

title: Lockheed P2V-7 · Reno, NV (2008)
summary: Just after the airplane's landing gear was retracted during takeoff for a retardant drop mission, a ball of fire was observed coming out of the left jet engine before the airplane rolled steeply to the left and descended into the terrain. title: Learjet LR60 · Columbia, SC (2008)
summary: The NTSB’s full report is available at http://www.ntsb.gov/publictn/publictn.htm. The Aircraft Accident Report number is NTSB/AAR-10/02. probable_cause: The operator’s inadequate maintenance of the airplane’s tires, which resulted in multiple tire failures during takeoff roll due to severe underinflation, and the captain’s execution of a rejected takeoff (RTO) after V1, which was inconsistent with her training and standard operating procedures. title: Aerospatiale SA365N-1 D · District Heights, MD (2008)
summary: The Safety Board's full report is available at http://www.ntsb.gov/Publictn/2009/AAR0907.pdf. The Aircraft Accident Report number is NTSB/AAR-09/07 On September 27, 2008, about 2358 eastern daylight time, an Aerospatiale (Eurocopter) SA365N1, N92MD, call sign Trooper 2, registered to and operated by the Maryland State Police (MSP) as a public medical evacuation flight, impacted terrain about 3.2 miles north of the runway 19R threshold at Andrews Air Force Base (ADW), Camp Springs, Maryland, during an instrument landing system approach. The commercial pilot, one flight paramedic, one field provider, and one of two automobile accident patients being transported were killed.
probable_cause: The pilot's attempt to regain visual conditions by performing a rapid descent and his failure to arrest the descent at the minimum descent altitude during a nonprecision approach. Contributing to the accident were (1) the pilot’s limited recent instrument flight experience, (2) the lack of adherence to effective risk management procedures by the Maryland State Police, (3) the pilot’s inadequate assessment of the weather, which led to his decision to accept the flight,, (4) the failure of the Potomac Consolidated Terminal Radar Approach Control (PCT) controller to provide the current Andrews Air Force Base weather observation to the pilot, and (5) the increased workload on the pilot due to inadequate Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control handling by the Ronald Reagan National Airport Tower and PCT controllers.

Metallurgical examination revealed that the NLG axle fractured in a transverse plane, and that the failure of the axle was due to intergranular cracking that acted as stress concentrators from which fatigue cracks emanated. The fracture of the right side inboard journal on the NLG inner cylinder assembly was most likely due to the failure of a prior tapered roller bearing.
probable_cause: The right nose landing gear axle's failure from intergranular and fatigue cracking due to an earlier bearing failure.

title: British Airways 38
summary: On approach to Heathrow, ice crystals that accumulated in the fuel during high-altitude cruise released back into the fuel system when the aircraft descended and demanded increased thrust. The ice froze in the fuel/oil heat exchanger of each Rolls-Royce Trent engine, restricting fuel flow and causing reduced engine response. The aircraft landed safely on grass 270 meters short of the runway with 47 injured.

title: Andersen Air Force Base B-2 accident
summary: The B-2 Spirit stealth bomber Spirit of Kansas crashed on the runway moments after takeoff from Andersen Air Force Base in Guam on 23 February 2008. Heavy, lashing rains caused moisture to enter skin-flush air-data sensors. Three pressure transducers failed to function due to condensation inside devices. Because of erroneous sensor data, the flight-control computers calculated inaccurate angle of attack and airspeed. The incorrect airspeed data led the aircraft to rotate 12 knots slower than indicated on the cockpit displays.

This combination caused an unrecoverable stall.

title: 2008 South Carolina Learjet 60 crash
summary: Learjet 60 N999LJ experienced multiple tire failures during takeoff roll on 19 September 2008. Captain aborted at 144 knots, exceeding the V1 decision speed of 136 knots. Tire debris damaged the hydraulic system and the air-ground sensing system. With hydraulics compromised and the air-ground sensor in air mode, reverse thrusters could not engage and main brakes failed. The aircraft overran the runway, crashed through the boundary fence and embankment, and caught fire. Inadequate tire pressure maintenance and a design flaw in the thrust reverser system contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: Severely under-inflated tires that burst during takeoff, tire debris damage to hydraulic system and air-ground sensor, and pilot's decision to abort after V1 decision speed

title: Qantas 72
summary: An Airbus A330 at cruise experienced two uncommanded pitch-down maneuvers caused by a faulty air data inertial reference unit (ADIRU) that corrupted angle-of-attack data, combined with a flight control computer software design limitation. The crew regained control and made a successful emergency landing at Learmonth Airport. Twelve crew and passengers suffered serious injuries.
probable_cause: A fault in ADIRU unit number one caused it to output corrupted angle-of-attack data by erroneously relabeling altitude information. The FCPC software had a design limitation that allowed multiple AOA spikes from a single ADIRU to trigger nose-down pitch commands, which the aircraft had no protection against in this specific rare condition.

factors.evidence: One of the three ADIRUs started providing incorrect data; the CPU erroneously relabeled altitude data representing 37,012 feet as an angle of attack of 50.625 degrees.
The FCPC software could not handle multiple spikes in AOA data from a single ADIRU in the specific rare situation, resulting in erroneous high-AOA protection mode activation.
The autopilot disengaged automatically when the ADIRU fault occurred, placing full control with the flight crew during the emergency.

Crew received contradictory stall and overspeed warnings, loss of altitude information on the primary flight display, and multiple electronic centralised aircraft monitor system warnings simultaneously.
Two uncommanded pitch-down maneuvers occurred reaching 8.4 degrees pitch down with 650 feet altitude loss on the first, and 3.5 degrees with 400 feet loss on the second.

events.text: ADIRU unit number one began providing incorrect data; autopilot disengaged automatically and crew received contradictory stall and overspeed warnings plus multiple system alerts.
First uncommanded pitch-down maneuver with minus 0.8 g acceleration, aircraft pitched down 8.4 degrees and rapidly lost 650 feet of altitude.
Crew recovered aircraft to assigned cruise flight level FL370 within 20 seconds of first maneuver.
Second uncommanded maneuver with plus 0.2 g acceleration, aircraft pitched down 3.5 degrees and lost 400 feet of altitude.
Crew re-established assigned level flight within 16 seconds; pilots declared state of alert and diverted to Learmonth Airport.

summary: DHC-6 Twin Otter Flight 101 crashed short of the runway at Tenzing-Hillary Airport in Lukla during a visual approach in bad weather. title: XL Airways Germany 888T

summary: XL Airways Flight 888T was an acceptance test flight of an Airbus A320 on 27 November 2008. Incorrect maintenance procedures allowed water to enter and freeze in the angle-of-attack sensors, rendering them inoperative. During descent, the crew attempted to perform a slow-flight test at approximately 8,000 to 6,000 feet, below the intended test altitude. The aircraft crashed into the Mediterranean Sea 7 km off the French coast, killing all seven people on board.
